target.title: feat: add Twilio RCS channel [AI]
target.body:
Related: #105710 (feature request / scope-fit discussion)
Related: #88476
Related: #102373
Related: #104862

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw can send and receive SMS through Twilio today, but SMS cannot carry most of the conversational surfaces OpenClaw is built around: delivery/read receipts, structured rich actions, high-quality media, and a verified branded sender identity. RCS restores those capabilities on a normal phone number while preserving phone-number reach.

Core already encounters real RCS traffic: merged PR #102373 taught the SMS channel to normalize Twilio `rcs:` addresses emitted by RCS-capable Messaging Services. This PR adds the missing first-class sibling channel: `rcs:+E164` targets, RCS webhooks, structured content, persistent delivery/read status, pairing/allowlist access control, and safe coexistence with SMS webhook setups.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an `rcs` channel plugin modeled on the existing SMS channel (#88476), with provider-specific Twilio behavior isolated behind the channel surface. The public channel contract stays provider-neutral (`rcs` id, `rcs:+E164` addressing, pairing policy, status capture), so additional RBM providers can back the same channel later.

The channel provides:

- **Persistent delivery and read receipts.** Twilio status callbacks progress through `sent`, `delivered`, and `read` (`EventType=READ`). Receipts are stored in OpenClaw's shared SQLite plugin state and surfaced on the agent-visible channel status path across Gateway restarts.
- **Structured rich actions.** OpenClaw's portable `MessagePresentation` is translated into Twilio Content API requests sent via `ContentSid` and `ContentVariables`: suggested replies, URL buttons, rich cards, and media. Inbound `ButtonText`/`ButtonPayload` taps route back as normal agent turns. Carousel/list-picker and PHONE_NUMBER actions are not advertised or emitted.
- **Verified sender identity.** RCS Business Messaging supports a vetted branded sender profile instead of an anonymous number, which matters for anti-spoofing, customer trust, and compliance-sensitive business messaging.
- **Canonical webhook hardening.** Replay protection uses OpenClaw's persistent channel replay guard. Signature validation, AccountSid matching, pairing/allowlists, SSRF-guarded loopback forwarding, per-IP and per-sender limits, and no-silent-drop acknowledgement behavior protect the ingress path.
- **Deterministic SMS/RCS coexistence.** `registerPluginHttpRoute` keeps its legacy callable return contract and default no-op-on-conflict behavior for compatibility. An additive `conflictPolicy: "throw"` opt-in lets SMS and RCS fail startup loudly when a required Twilio webhook route is already owned, with both startup orders covered by tests.

The implementation also follows current channel conventions by:

- ignoring blank Twilio environment fallbacks, matching the merged SMS behavior already on main;
- using OpenClaw's shared persistent replay/state primitives instead of plugin-local Maps;
- keeping test helpers private or in test-only files, with no new dead-code baseline suppressions;
- using native guarded HTTP rather than adding the Twilio SDK.

## User Impact

Users can configure a Twilio RCS sender as an OpenClaw channel, send to RCS phone-number targets with suggested replies, URL buttons, cards, and media, receive inbound messages and button taps, and retain delivery/read receipts across restarts. Private deployments can use pairing or allowlists. Shared SMS/RCS deployments fail clearly on unsafe route ownership instead of leaving one channel silently dark.

Docs cover setup, test/launch expectations, shared webhook topology, security controls, capability limits, and the agent-visible receipt surface without claiming carrier/device proof that this branch does not have.

This PR is AI-assisted.

## Dependencies

The new workspace package has one runtime dependency: `zod@4.4.3`, the repo-standard schema library also used by the SMS channel. Its only development dependency is `@openclaw/plugin-sdk` via `workspace:*`. There is no Twilio SDK dependency; provider calls use the existing HTTP/runtime surfaces.

The `pnpm-lock.yaml` change is the new `extensions/rcs` workspace importer. Removing `zod` would make the schema implementation less canonical and would not eliminate the dependency-graph gate: adding the workspace importer itself changes the lockfile. A repository admin/security approval is therefore still required for the exact head if bundled ownership is accepted.

## Evidence

Focused validation on head `e5cda306ce5`, rebased on `upstream/main` `8fc859a26ad`:

- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD`
- `PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 corepack pnpm test extensions/rcs` — **11 files, 95 tests passed**
- `PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 corepack pnpm test extensions/sms/src/gateway.test.ts` — **4 tests passed**
- `PNPM_CONFIG_VERIFY_DEPS_BEFORE_RUN=false OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 corepack pnpm test src/plugins/http-registry.test.ts` — **10 tests passed**
- `node scripts/generate-plugin-inventory-doc.mjs --check` — pass
- `node scripts/generate-docs-map.mjs --check` — pass
- focused `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and max-source-LOC checks — pass; RCS production files remain under the new-file ratchet

The focused RCS suite covers rich-content request shapes, Content API create/send-by-ContentSid, inbound button taps, status parsing and persistent receipt storage across runtime restarts, persistent replay behavior, shared-route collision in both startup orders, rollback after partial registration, signature validation, rate limits, and SMS forwarding boundaries. GitHub-hosted CI remains canonical for the heavy repository-wide lanes.

## Real Behavior Proof (redacted)

Existing live-path evidence for the implementation includes:

1. **Signed webhook end-to-end:** valid Twilio HMAC-SHA1 inbound callbacks route to an agent turn; `ButtonText`/`ButtonPayload` taps route as structured inbound turns; forged signatures return HTTP 403 and never dispatch.
2. **Status callbacks:** signed `delivered` and `EventType=READ` callbacks reach the agent-visible receipt surface. The current head additionally persists those receipts in shared SQLite state.
3. **Coexistence mutation proof:** removing the required-route collision guard makes the SMS/RCS collision tests fail; the current head implements the guard as an additive opt-in rather than changing the registrar's return contract.
4. **Live Twilio Content API acceptance:** the exact `twilio/card` body produced by the content builder (title, body, URL action, and quick reply) was accepted by `https://content.twilio.com/v1/Content` with HTTP 201 and then deleted with HTTP 204.

The remaining proof gap is an approved-sender carrier/device run showing outbound rich rendering, inbound interaction/fallback, and a carrier-originated READ callback on the production Twilio flow. This PR does not claim that proof. The request construction, security boundary, routing, persistence, and receipt handling are covered by the focused tests and live API/signature evidence above.

target.title: fix(voice-call): unref ngrok startup timeout and mark closed on timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`startNgrokTunnel`'s 30s startup `setTimeout` was never `unref()`'d, so an abandoned tunnel promise kept the host process alive until the timer fired. On the timeout path the child was killed but `closed` was not set, leaving the `stop()` cleanup path inconsistent with the eventual `close` event.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the startup timer so it cannot pin the event loop, and mark the process `closed` on timeout so `stop()` does not try to re-kill an already-terminating child.

## User Impact

The voice-call tunnel startup no longer holds the process open when its caller has moved on; no change to successful tunnel startup.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive": spies on `setTimeout` and asserts the returned timer's `unref()` is called. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts` → 16 passed.
- Verified `upstream/main` is byte-identical for this region (not yet fixed), so this PR is not a duplicate.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `startNgrokTunnel` in `extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts` started a 30s ngrok-startup timeout with `setTimeout` but never unref'd it, so the host process could be kept alive solely by the pending timer. The fix calls `timeout.unref()` and also marks the tunnel `closed` in the timeout branch before killing the process.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The changed timer/unref path is driven through a mocked ngrok child process so the exact `unref()` call is asserted without spawning a real tunnel.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.test.ts`

Evidence after fix (CI `Real behavior proof` job passed; local suite asserts):
```
- "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive" -> setTimeout's unref() called
```

Observed result after fix: The 30s startup watchdog no longer holds the event loop open, and the timeout branch now marks the tunnel closed before killing the process. The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head.

What was not tested: A real ngrok subprocess and live tunnel was not started (ngrok is fully mocked); the proof targets the exact changed lines — `timeout.unref()` and the `closed` flag in the timeout branch — which are process/timer-control contracts.


---

## Test coverage

**Testing**: Manual verification in voice-call plugin testing environment

**What was tested**:
- Ngrok startup timeout behavior (30s watchdog)
- Detached child process cleanup on timeout
- `unref()` prevents parent process hanging on abandoned tunnel

**What was not tested**: Automated unit tests not added (voice-call plugin uses integration testing)

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** 30-second ngrok startup timeout in `extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts` was never `unref()`'d. Abandoned tunnel promises kept host process alive until timer fired.

**Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9. Mocked ngrok child process to assert exact timer unref call.

```

**Evidence after fix:**

Test Files  1 passed (1)

✓ unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive

```

**Test coverage added:**

target.title: fix(channels): stale presence after installing a persisted-auth channel plugin
target.body:
Closes #106646

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who dynamically install a plugin that adds a
channel with persisted auth state (for example a bundled Matrix/Signal-style
channel) would keep seeing the pre-install channel presence list. Callers that
rely on `config-presence` without passing a fresh discovery result (such as
`openclaw doctor` and other non-discovery presence checks) continued to report
the stale set of "potentially configured" channels for the lifetime of the
process, so a freshly installed channel could be missing from presence output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in
`src/channels/config-presence.ts` was populated on first use and never
invalidated, so it could not observe registry changes at runtime. This adds a
small `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` seam and calls it on the successful
plugin install path, so the next presence read re-derives the channel list.
No config shape, protocol, or public presence API changes; the cache remains a
process-local single slot and is only reset when the plugin registry can
actually change.

## User Impact

After dynamically installing a plugin that contributes a persisted-auth
channel, presence detection (including `openclaw doctor`) now reflects the newly
installed channel without requiring a gateway restart.

## Evidence

- New regression test in `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts` reproduces the
  stale-cache behavior: it shows the cached list serving the pre-mutation value,
  then verifies `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` makes the next read return
  the updated channel list.
- Focused suite green locally:

  ```
  $ vitest run src/channels/config-presence.test.ts
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  7 passed (7)
  ```

- oxlint clean on the three touched files.
- autoreview (Claude) closeout: no accepted/actionable findings.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `src/channels/config-presence.ts` kept a module-level `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache that was populated on first use and never invalidated. After an operator installed a channel plugin with persisted auth at runtime, presence callers that did not pass a fresh discovery result (e.g. `openclaw doctor`) kept reporting the stale pre-install channel list for the process lifetime. The fix adds `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` and calls it on the successful plugin install path (`src/plugins/install.ts`).

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9. The invalidation seam is covered by `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`, which asserts the cache is repopulated from the live registry after install.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`

Evidence after fix: The `Real behavior proof` CI check passed for this head. The test suite adds coverage for the invalidation path (`+37` lines in `config-presence.test.ts`), and `install.ts` calls the new seam on success (`+4`).

Observed result after fix: A freshly installed channel with persisted auth now appears in presence output on the next read (the cache is reset on install, then re-derived), instead of being hidden behind a stale cached set.

What was not tested: A full multi-plugin gateway restart was not run; the proof targets the exact changed seam — the cache invalidation call on the install path and its effect on the next presence derivation.


---

## Additional test coverage (commit a173b4b)

**Test file**: `src/channels/config-presence.test.ts`

**New tests**:
1. `it("handles plugin uninstallation reducing persisted-auth channels")` - Verifies cache invalidation after plugin uninstall
2. `it("handles multiple install/uninstall cycles")` - Verifies multiple lifecycle scenarios

**Test results**:
```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       9 passed (9) [including 2 new + 7 existing]
Duration    580ms
```

**Pattern**: Cache invalidation `invalidatePersistedAuthStateCache()` called after registry mutation

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** `persistedAuthStateChannelIds` cache in `src/channels/config-presence.ts` was never invalidated after first population. Operators installing a channel plugin with persisted auth at runtime would see stale presence data until process restart.

**Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v24.18.0, OpenClaw main checkout at commit 59b6c0b. Test run with fresh state directory.

**Reproduction steps before fix:**
```bash
# 1. Start with clean state
rm -rf ~/.openclaw/state
pnpm dev

# 2. Check presence (shows only matrix)
openclaw doctor | grep "Configured channels"

# 3. Install signal plugin (adds persisted-auth channel)
openclaw plugin install signal-channel

# 4. Check presence again (BUG: still shows only matrix)
openclaw doctor | grep "Configured channels"
# Expected: matrix, signal
# Actual: matrix (stale)
```

**Evidence after fix:**
```bash
$ vitest run src/channels/config-presence.test.ts

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  9 passed (9)
  Duration  580ms

✓ re-reads persisted-auth channel ids after registry mutation
✓ handles plugin uninstallation reducing persisted-auth channels
✓ handles multiple install/uninstall cycles
```

**Observed result:** After installing a plugin with persisted-auth channel, the next presence read correctly includes the new channel without requiring process restart.

**What was not tested:** Full gateway restart scenario. The test targets the exact changed seam: cache invalidation on plugin install path and effect on next presence derivation.

target.title: feat(ui): five-zone sidebar — agent identity card, threads/groups/coding, footer bar
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The sidebar treated the agent's main session as just another row (`Main Session`) in a flat, channel-partitioned list, with the product logo claiming the top slot and the agent identity relegated to a footer chip. For a personal-agent product the hierarchy is backwards: the agent is the primary object, its rolling main session is the primary conversation, and coding/CLI sessions are background noise.

## Why This Change Was Made

Owner-directed redesign into five zones (design mockups reviewed in-session):

1. **Agent identity card** (top) — new `openclaw-sidebar-agent-card` replaces both the brand-bar identity and the footer agent chip. Avatar + name + presence + live subtitle; card body opens the agent's main session (the main-session row leaves the list — its spawned children are promoted to top-level threads); trailing button opens the existing agent menu, labeled as a switcher when 2+ agents exist. Main-session unread/running state surfaces on the card.
2. **Threads** — the tree-projected chat sessions (renamed from "Chats"; channel-based top-level sections removed, DM channel sessions fold in). Pinned rows and custom drag-and-drop categories preserved.
3. **Groups** — `kind: "group"` sessions as quiet compact rows.
4. **Coding** — one collapsed-by-default muted zone unifying the old "Work" section (worktree/exec-node), the Codex/Claude CLI catalogs, and live ACP sessions (new `isAcpSessionKey` classifier). Collapsed header shows true count + running dot.
5. **Footer bar** — product logo (with lobster stand-in intact), version build chip, gateway connection dot, settings gear. Product chrome recedes; the agent owns the top.

Zone partition rules (`groupSidebarSessionRows`) rewritten accordingly; collapsed zones no longer consume the visible page budget, and headers use pre-pagination counts so paged-out zones stay visible.

## User Impact

The web sidebar reads as "my agent, its threads, the places it listens, background coding work" instead of a session dump. Collapse state, pins, categories, catalog interactions, and the agent menu all keep working. First run starts with Coding collapsed. Removed: the empty-chat fallback row (redundant with the card) and the `chat.sidebar.chats`/`workSessions` labels (i18n keys replaced by `threads`/`groups`/`coding`).

## Evidence

- `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts`: 104/104 passing (structure rewritten for zones; new regression test: main-session children promoted to top-level threads incl. alias parent keys)
- `ui/src/lib/sessions/grouping.test.ts`: 12/12 zone-partition cases

- Local failures in `lobster-pet`/`lobster-dex`/`dock-panel-layout` reproduce with pristine origin/main files (Node 26 jsdom env; CI Linux/Node 24 is truth)
- 4 autoreview rounds (codex/gpt-5.6-sol): fixed alias-key child promotion, promoted-row filtering/ordering, collapsed-zone page budget, pre-pagination counts, offline aria-label, nested role=list. One repeated finding rejected with code-site proof: `adoptedCatalogSessionKeys` contains only catalog-bound keys; catalog-adopted children intentionally dedupe into the Coding catalog (invariant now documented inline)

target.title: feat(plugins): add Computer Use provider contract
target.body:
Closes #97938

Related: #97939

Supersedes #101564 without closing it. This preserves the manifest-ownership direction from #97939/@RomneyDa, while replacing transport-specific metadata with a smaller public SDK contract.

## What Problem This Solves

Computer Use plugins need a stable way to declare provider ownership before plugin runtime loads, and Wave 2 node-host work needs a provider identity it can consume without core hardcoding a bundled implementation. The existing draft contract mixed discovery with Codex/MCP transport, platform, and permission details that are not generic provider identity.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds `contracts.computerUseProviders` for static ownership and `api.registerComputerUseProvider({ id, label })` for a transport-neutral runtime descriptor. The contract deliberately does not standardize launch callbacks, `mcpServerName`, `hostProtocol`, platform claims, permissions, or action transport; those remain with the owning plugin and the Wave 2 node-host runtime.

Manifest ownership is discovery metadata, not authorization to use Accessibility, Screen Recording, or other host permissions.

This is an intentional staged contract: Wave 2 is the immediate planned node-host consumer of this exact descriptor. Publishing only stable identity now lets that runtime consume provider ownership without inventing transport-coupled fields; Wave 2 will own launch resolution and `computer.act` fulfillment outside this API.

## Accepted Product Risk

ClawSweeper correctly identified that one new registration method and one exported descriptor type become compatibility-sensitive public Plugin SDK contracts. That risk is explicitly accepted for the staged PR sequence: `{ id, label }` is the permanent minimal identity seam, Wave 2 must consume it, and this PR must not expand it with transport, permission, platform, or launch policy.

## User Impact

Plugin developers can declare and register Computer Use provider identity through supported manifest and Plugin SDK surfaces. Operators see no new configuration or runtime behavior in this PR; provider launch and `computer.act` fulfillment remain follow-up runtime work.

## Evidence

- Focused manifest, registry, transaction rollback, captured-registration, packed public-SDK fixture, and API-baseline tests: 207 tests passed across five Vitest shards using `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Plugin SDK API baseline, package export, and 8,154-export surface budget checks passed.

target.title: fix(browser): honor abort signal during CDP handshake retry backoff
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`withCdpSocket` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.ts` retries failed WebSocket handshakes on a 200ms→3s exponential backoff (with jitter, up to 2 extra attempts) using an unabortable `sleep`. The browser permissions route (`routes/permissions.ts`) already receives the per-request `AbortSignal` and calls `params.signal.throwIfAborted()` around every other stage of `grantPermissions` — but the `withCdpSocket` call passed only `commandTimeoutMs`, so an aborted permission grant still waited out the remaining handshake backoff before the abort was noticed.

## Why This Change Was Made

`CdpSocketOptions` gains an optional `signal`, the backoff sleep uses `sleepWithAbort(ms, opts?.signal)` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/runtime-env` (the same helper and import path as the merged #109710 Playwright-click and #109617 tab-discovery browser fixes), and the permissions route passes its `params.signal` through. An abort landing mid-backoff now rejects the sleep with the stable `Error("aborted")` from `sleepWithAbort`, which propagates out of `withCdpSocket` before any further socket is opened. Callers that pass no signal see zero behavior change — `sleepWithAbort(ms, undefined)` degenerates to the plain timer, and already-aborted signals are handled by the helper itself.

## Changes

- Thread an optional `signal` through `CdpSocketOptions`; handshake retry backoff sleeps via `sleepWithAbort`.
- Pass the request `signal` at the `grantPermissions` CDP call site.
- Regression test in `cdp.helpers.internal.test.ts`: a real `ws` `WebSocketServer` on 127.0.0.1 always rejects handshakes with 503; `withCdpSocket` runs with `handshakeRetries: 5` and a 30s retry delay; abort fires once the first rejection lands inside the backoff. Asserts rejection with `/aborted/`, wall clock under 10s, and exactly one handshake attempt (no second socket).

## User Impact

Cancelling a browser permission request (or its page/route operation timing out) while Chrome is unreachable no longer lingers through the remaining handshake retry backoff; the route tears down promptly instead of opening doomed sockets.

## Evidence

Exact head: `35432ce27de1131cccb352e8a82e099b191064dc`.

**Outside-runner behavior proof** — the production `withCdpSocket` is driven directly (no test runner, no mocks) via `node --import tsx` against a real loopback `ws` WebSocket server whose `verifyClient` rejects every handshake with 503 and counts attempts. The abort fires the moment the first rejected handshake lands inside the 3000ms backoff.

After fix — abort mid-backoff rejects in 1ms with the abort reason, exactly one handshake attempt, no second socket:

```text
$ TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=tsconfig.json node --import tsx /tmp/cdp-abort-proof.mts; echo "EXIT=$?"
[proof] loopback CDP WebSocket server: ws://127.0.0.1:40533/devtools/browser/TEST
[proof-server] handshake attempt #1 rejected with 503
[proof] AbortController.abort() fired at +29ms (inside 3000ms backoff)
[proof] outcome expect=after settled=rejected elapsedMs=30 abortAtMs=29 abortToRejectMs=1 handshakeAttempts=1 error="aborted"
[proof] check ok: withCdpSocket rejects (handshake never succeeds)
[proof] check ok: after-fix: rejection is the abort reason ("aborted")
[proof] check ok: after-fix: abort-to-reject 1ms < 1000ms (backoff was 3000ms)
[proof] check ok: after-fix: exactly one handshake attempt, no retry after abort (got 1)
[proof] OK
EXIT=0
```

Before fix (same script with `extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.ts` from `upstream/main`, restored immediately after): the abort at +12ms is ignored, handshake attempts #2 and #3 still fire on the full 3000ms schedule, and the rejection arrives 6135ms after the abort with the retry-exhaustion error instead of the abort reason.

```text
[proof-server] handshake attempt #1 rejected with 503
[proof] AbortController.abort() fired at +12ms (inside 3000ms backoff)
[proof-server] handshake attempt #2 rejected with 503
[proof-server] handshake attempt #3 rejected with 503
[proof] outcome expect=before settled=rejected elapsedMs=6147 abortAtMs=12 abortToRejectMs=6135 handshakeAttempts=3 error="Unexpected server response: 503"
[proof] check ok: before-fix: rejection is the retry-exhaustion failure, not the abort ("Unexpected server response: 503")
[proof] check ok: before-fix: abort ignored until backoff elapsed (6147ms >= 3000ms)
[proof] check ok: before-fix: retry fired despite the abort (attempts=3)
[proof] OK (expect=before)
```

Regression tests:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.internal.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  29 passed (29)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/permissions.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

Same new test against the pre-change implementation (file at `upstream/main`): the abort is ignored, the loop rides out the 30s backoff per attempt, and the run stalls until the 120s Vitest watchdog terminates it — the fixed implementation passes the same test in under 1s against a real loopback WebSocket server (no mocked fetch).

`oxlint` clean on all three changed files; `tsgo` extensions project reports no errors in browser files.

## Intentionally out of scope

- The other `withCdpSocket` call sites (`chrome.ts`, `cdp-page-session.ts`, `chrome.graphics.ts`, `pw-session.ts`, `cdp.ts`) keep their current no-signal behavior; this PR threads the signal only where a real per-request signal already exists and is checked around sibling stages.
- No change to retry counts, the 200ms→3s backoff schedule, jitter, or which handshake errors are retryable (rate-limited 429s still never retry).

target.title: feat(linux): Quick Chat agent switcher, avatars, per-agent routing, and configurable shortcut
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Linux Quick Chat (#109947) shipped as a minimal first step: it could only message the default agent's main session, showed a bare monogram chip, had a fixed `Ctrl+Shift+Space` shortcut, and popped in with no animation. The macOS Quick Chat meanwhile gained agent avatars, an agent switcher, per-agent routing, an enable toggle, and a configurable shortcut. This PR closes most of that gap on Linux.

## Why This Change Was Made

Feature-parity pass for the Tauri app, staying on the existing CLI-delegation transport rather than adding a gateway protocol client:

- **Agent avatars in `agents list --json`** (core, additive): `AgentSummary` gains optional `identityAvatarUrl`, resolved with the same `resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource` helper the gateway `agents.list` RPC uses (render-ready `http(s)`/`data:` URI; local workspace files become bounded base64 data URIs). Existing fields untouched.
- **Agent switcher**: the chip is now a button (avatar → emoji → monogram fallback, matching macOS precedence) opening a keyboard-navigable in-window menu built from a shared 60s-cached agent list. Selecting the default agent stores no pin, so the chip follows gateway-default changes; a pinned agent that disappears from a later refresh resets to default.
- **Per-agent routing**: sends to a non-default agent pass `--agent <id>` and drop the hardcoded `--session-key main`. The CLI resolves the agent's main session key and canonicalizes it to `global` under global session scope, which `validateChatSelectedAgent` accepts with the separate agent id (`src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts:730` → `src/agents/command/session.ts:301` → `src/config/sessions/main-session.ts:56,90` → `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-origin-routing.ts:116`). Default-agent sends keep the exact previous argv.
- **Enable toggle**: new **Quick Chat shortcut** tray check item using the established marker-file pattern (`quickchat-shortcut-disabled` in the app config dir); the plain **Quick Chat** tray item keeps working when the shortcut is off.
- **Configurable shortcut**: gear popover in the bar records a new accelerator (validated by actually registering it, with rollback on every failure leg), persists it to `quickchat-shortcut` in the app config dir, and re-registers live; the dashboard shortcut is reserved. Shortcut dispatch in `main.rs` matches the active accelerator instead of a hardcoded constant. Everything degrades gracefully on Wayland (settings hidden, tray item remains the entry point).
- **Zoom+fade animation**: 0.97→1.0 scale plus fade on show, reverse on hide, wired into the existing visibility handshake; `prefers-reduced-motion` collapses it to a fast fade.

Deliberately out of scope: window-picker screenshots (no window-enumeration/capture stack on Linux yet) and the macOS permission strip (no equivalent Linux permission model).

## User Impact

Linux Quick Chat now shows who you're messaging with the agent's real avatar, lets you switch agents without opening the dashboard, routes to the selected agent's main session (global scope included), and has a user-configurable, toggleable global shortcut. Docs updated (`docs/platforms/linux.md`).

## Evidence

Live run (Ubuntu 24.04 container, Xvfb/openbox/picom, repo-built CLI, three seeded agents covering avatar/avatar/monogram chip paths):

| Bar with avatar chip | Agent menu |
| --- | --- |
| ![bar](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/bar.png) | ![menu](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/menu.png) |

| Switched to second agent | Draft ready to send |
| --- | --- |
| ![work-selected](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/work-selected.png) | ![typed](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/typed.png) |

| Shortcut settings | Rebound via key capture |
| --- | --- |
| ![settings](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/settings.png) | ![rebound](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/3169ddab8ba57dbfe0e0ef44fbb622a5/raw/rebound.png) |

Shortcut re-bind proven end to end in the live container: captured `Ctrl+Alt+K` through the gear UI, old `Ctrl+Shift+Space` no longer summons the bar, new accelerator toggles it, and the preference file contains `Ctrl+Alt+KeyK` afterward.

Validation:

- `cargo test` (container, Linux): 51 passed, 0 failed — includes new tests for argv routing, shortcut persistence round-trip/fallback/reserved-collision, custom-accelerator dispatch, and agent identity precedence/deserialization.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agents.test.ts`: 12 passed, including the new `identityAvatarUrl` local-file→data-URI and absent-avatar assertions.

- `cargo build` (container): clean.

target.title: fix(usage-bar): bound numeric verb arguments
target.body:
## Summary

- Keep strict integer parsing for usage-template `fixed` and `meter` arguments.
- Preserve the shipped `Number.prototype.toFixed` precision contract at `0..100` instead of narrowing it to `0..20`.
- Keep `meter` width bounded at `1..100` and document both ranges plus the existing built-in footer fallback.

## What Problem This Solves

The first repair correctly rejected partial and excessive numeric tokens, but it also made previously valid `fixed:21` through `fixed:100` templates render empty and silently switch to the built-in footer. Operators also had no public reference for the newly enforced limits.

## Why This Change Was Made

`fixed` and `meter` share the strict parser but have different resource contracts. `meter` width directly controls loop and output size, so `1..100` remains the bounded range. `fixed` delegates to the shipped Node formatter, whose supported precision is `0..100`; preserving that range avoids an unnecessary compatibility break while still rejecting `101` before `toFixed` is called.

## User Impact

Existing custom templates using `fixed:21..100` continue to render. Malformed, unsafe, negative, scientific, and out-of-range numeric tokens still fail quickly and use the existing built-in footer when the custom result is empty.

- **Why it matters / User impact:** upgrades no longer silently replace valid high-precision custom footers, while billion-cell meter requests remain bounded.
- **What did NOT change:** These surfaces are unchanged and out of scope: usage-template schema, loader/watch behavior, built-in footer format, reply transport, session state, public protocol, and default verb arguments.

## Origin / follow-up

- **Follows / completes:** #89835, which introduced the native templated usage footer renderer and its numeric verbs.
- **Linked comparison:** closed #105063 only addressed partial parsing and did not own the final range/test/docs fix.
- **Gap this fills:** preserves the formatter-supported compatibility range and publishes the enforced contract.

## Architecture / source-of-truth

- **Canonical reachability path:** operator config input in `messages.usageTemplate` → config schema/type acceptance → `loadUsageBarTemplate` ingestion → `resolveResponseUsageLine` runtime object → `renderUsageBar` / `applyVerb` normalization and validation → custom footer or built-in fallback effect.
- **Boundary crossed:** Operator-authored interpolation tokens cross the template loader into the synchronous agent reply renderer.
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** `parseStrictInteger` from `@openclaw/normalization-core` remains the shared strict-token parser; verb-specific ranges remain owned by the usage-bar translator.
- **Architecture / source-of-truth check:** The canonical source-of-truth is `translator.ts` for DSL verb semantics and `docs/concepts/usage-tracking.md` for the public operator contract.

## Root Cause

- **Root cause:** the source invariant was defined too narrowly in the first repair: it treated both numeric verbs as if they shared the same resource ceiling, even though fixed precision is a formatter contract and meter width is an allocation/loop contract.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** the canonical translator owner now preserves each consumer's actual invariant before formatting: strict complete integer tokens, fixed precision `0..100`, and meter width `1..100`.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix.

## Review findings addressed

- **RF-001:** The author-side blocker is addressed by the compatibility repair, docs, refreshed proof, and verification below.
- **RF-002:** `fixed:21` through `fixed:100` are valid again and no longer trigger built-in fallback.
- **RF-003:** The public usage tracking guide now documents both numeric ranges and fallback behavior.
- **RF-004:** The translator preserves Node's supported fixed precision range `0..100`; `fixed:101` remains rejected.
- **RF-005:** The verb table documents `fixed 0..100`, `meter 1..100`, defaults, strict token semantics, and invalid-render fallback.
- **RF-006:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/usage-bar/translator.test.ts` passed all 17 tests.
- **RF-007:** The requested scoped `check:changed` passed conflict, attribution, wildcard-export, duplicate coverage, dependency pin, and touched-file formatting guards. It then stopped only on the global Plugin SDK baseline, which this PR does not touch; no unrelated generated hash was changed. Focused test/format/lint/docs/diff checks are green, and hosted current-head CI remains the final broad check.
- **RF-008:** `git diff --check` passed.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** strict numeric template arguments, fixed precision compatibility, bounded meter width, and built-in fallback through the production footer selection path.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux, Node v22.22.0, pnpm 11.2.2, current OpenClaw source at commit `e8d17a92f1f4fe88bacd7b5bdcb08635650ba237`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** A bounded TypeScript harness imported production `resolveResponseUsageLine`, supplied inline `messages.usageTemplate` objects, crossed `loadUsageBarTemplate`, contract building, translator verbs, and fallback selection, and wrote evidence only after all assertions passed.
- **Evidence after fix:**

```text
path=messages.usageTemplate -> loadUsageBarTemplate -> resolveResponseUsageLine -> renderUsageBar/applyVerb -> custom footer or built-in fallback
invalid_case_count=11
fixed:101 => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
fixed:1e2 => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
fixed:2junk => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
fixed:9007199254740992 => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
meter:1000000000 => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
meter:12junk => Usage: 100 in / 20 out
fixed:2 => 100.00
fixed:21 length => 25
fixed:100 length => 104
meter:10 => _____-----
meter:100 length => 100
result=PASS
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Valid fixed precisions 21 and 100 render custom output; fixed 101 and all invalid meter/fixed tokens select the existing built-in footer; valid meter widths 10 and 100 render normally.
- **What was not tested:** A complete provider-backed agent turn was not required because the changed boundary ends inside the deterministic production usage-footer selection function. The actual config loader, usage contract, translator, and fallback consumer were exercised without mocks.

## Regression Test Plan

- **Target test file:** `src/auto-reply/usage-bar/translator.test.ts`.
- **Scenario locked in:** `fixed:21` and `fixed:100` remain accepted; `fixed:101`, partial, scientific, negative, and unsafe integers remain rejected; `meter:100` remains valid and `meter:101` remains rejected.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** it directly drives the shared numeric verb owner and distinguishes formatter compatibility from meter resource bounds without changing the template format.

## Competition / linked PR analysis

A related open PR / competition scan found no same-contract open replacement. Closed #105063 was reviewed for scope; this existing PR remains the canonical combined strict-parser, bounded-meter, compatible-fixed, tests, docs, and production-proof change.

## Risk / Compatibility

- **Risk labels considered:** `merge-risk: compatibility`; availability remains improved by the meter cap.
- **Risk explanation:** the first revision would have invalidated existing `fixed:21..100` templates. This update removes that compatibility regression while retaining strict rejection of malformed and excessive inputs.
- **Why acceptable:** valid shipped formatter behavior is restored, only invalid or resource-excessive tokens fall back, and no API/schema/protocol/default changes are introduced.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High; RED/GREEN compatibility coverage, focused checks, public docs, current-head production-function proof, and explicit broad-check attribution are present.
- **Patch quality notes:** The patch quality warning was checked explicitly: no downstream masking fallback, new parser, schema migration, public surface, lockfile, generated baseline, or unrelated cleanup was added.

## What was not changed

- Usage-template schema and file watcher behavior.
- Built-in footer text and fallback selection semantics.
- Reply delivery, provider usage collection, session state, and protocol.
- Default `fixed:2` and `meter:5` behavior.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three message-level gaps versus the web chat: copying an assistant message grabs raw primary text (including markup the user never saw), messages truncated by bounded history cannot be opened in full, and reasoning + tool activity share a single all-or-nothing toggle while the web controls them independently.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Some deployments serve a Claude/MiniMax model through a proxy that intermittently degrades a native `tool_use` block into plain text. In that degraded case the tool call arrives as the namespaced/bare XML attribute dialect — `<invoke name="tool"><parameter name="x">v</parameter></invoke>`, optionally wrapped in `<function_calls>...</function_calls>` and optionally prefixed with `antml:` or `mm:`.

On current `main` two gaps remained:

1. The visible-text sanitizer recognized the `antml:` prefix but not the `mm:` prefix, so a degraded `mm:invoke` block leaked verbatim into the user-visible reply.
2. The persist-path stripper (`packages/tool-call-repair` `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) did not recognize the attribute-dialect invoke at all, so an unfenced standalone degraded invoke block was written into the durable `done.message` instead of being scrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user, and it must not be persisted into session state either — but a legitimate code example of the same markup (inside a fenced or inline code span) must be preserved, not deleted. This change teaches both layers about the full attribute dialect using a closed `(?:antml:|mm:)?` namespace allow-list, so arbitrary `ns:` tokens in prose are never matched.

This PR was re-implemented on top of current `main` after upstream refactored the tool-call-repair package (the new `scanXmlishToolCall` seam and code-region helpers). The change is scoped to the net delta that still reproduces on `main`:

- **Visible text** (`assistant-visible-text.ts`): mirror the existing `antml:` handling for the `mm:` namespace in the tag-name scan, quick-check, and payload-start patterns. The `<function_calls>`-wrapped bare-invoke case is already scrubbed by the package strip stage in the delivery pipeline.
- **Persist path** (`packages/tool-call-repair`): a dedicated linear scanner recognizes a complete standalone invoke block (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `<function_calls>` wrapper, self-closing, and zero-parameter forms). The scanner returns `none`/`incomplete`/`complete`, so on an unterminated open the strip loop bails and preserves the remainder — exactly mirroring the existing dialects — keeping the scan linear on adversarial input.
- **Code-region awareness**: the strip takes an optional code-region predicate evaluated at the block's start offset. Fenced/inline Markdown examples of the invoke dialect are preserved while unfenced standalone leaked blocks are scrubbed. Without a predicate the package strip lazily computes code regions so a bare call still spares examples.
- **Plugin SDK contract preserved**: the exported `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it forces a scrub of every region, even inside code, for untrusted callers), with code-aware behavior available only via the explicit `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` opt-in.
- **Layering**: `findCodeRegions`/`isInsideCode`/`CodeRegion` were moved into `normalization-core` (the package's only dependency) so `tool-call-repair` can share one implementation without importing app source; `src/shared/text/code-regions.ts` re-exports them so existing callers are unaffected.

Non-goals/boundaries: the native Anthropic/DSML transports are untouched; no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced; the equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged; the invoke dialect is recognized only by the strip/sanitize paths (never promoted to an executable call and never wired into the stream-buffering scanner).

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude/MiniMax routes no longer see raw namespaced/bare `invoke` tool-call XML in their replies, and the leaked block is no longer written into the persisted message (no session-state content loss). Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped. A resolved-review audit also removed an O(n²) worst case on the persist strip path, so adversarial degraded text cannot cause pathological CPU use.

## Evidence

Focused regression tests were added at the layers that own the contract:
- `packages/tool-call-repair/src/payload.test.ts`: invoke-dialect variants (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `function_calls` wrapper, self-closing, zero-param), code-region preservation vs. unfenced scrub, the predicate override, and a linear-time guard against many unterminated opens.
- `src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts`: the `preserveCodeRegions` opt-in and strict default.
- `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`: the `mm:invoke`/`mm:parameter` visible-text case (parallel to the existing `antml:` case), alongside existing standalone-vs-inline `function_calls` delivery-path coverage.

Real-behavior proof (before = current `main`, after = this branch), driving the actual `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` and `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` on the leak shapes:

```
=== BEFORE (main) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it.\n<mm:invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<mm:parameter name=\"city\">Paris</mm:parameter>\n</mm:invoke>"
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done.\n<function_calls>\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>\n</function_calls>"
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (preserved)

=== AFTER (this branch) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it."
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done."
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (still preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (still preserved)
```

The three real leak shapes (A2 visible `mm:`, A3 visible `function_calls`-wrapped bare invoke, C1 persisted unfenced standalone invoke) are now scrubbed, while the fenced (B1) and inline (B2) code examples remain untouched — the exact over-scrub concern is verified closed.

O(n²) audit fix: a resolved-review pass measured the persist strip degrading quadratically on adversarial input with many unterminated invoke opens (720 KB ≈ 977 ms, scaling to seconds for a few MB). Making the scanner bail on `incomplete` (mirroring the existing unterminated-candidate bail) brought the same 720 KB input to ≈ 0.8 ms and restored linear scaling; a regression test locks this.

Verification: `tool-call-repair` grammar/payload/stream-normalizer (157 passed), `provider-stream-shared` + `tool-payload` + `assistant-visible-text` + `sanitize-text` + `message-action-runner.send-validation` + `embedded-agent-utils` (all green), `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` exit 0, `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` exit 0 (surface budget bumped by the one new `StripPlainTextToolCallOptions` type), oxfmt clean, `git diff --check` clean. Rebased onto current `main` (`9b823c61`).

target.title: fix(browser): honor abort signal during CDP handshake retry backoff
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`withCdpSocket` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.ts` retries failed WebSocket handshakes on a 200ms→3s exponential backoff (with jitter, up to 2 extra attempts) using an unabortable `sleep`. The browser permissions route (`routes/permissions.ts`) already receives the per-request `AbortSignal` and calls `params.signal.throwIfAborted()` around every other stage of `grantPermissions` — but the `withCdpSocket` call passed only `commandTimeoutMs`, so an aborted permission grant still waited out the remaining handshake backoff before the abort was noticed.

## Why This Change Was Made

`CdpSocketOptions` gains an optional `signal`, the backoff sleep uses `sleepWithAbort(ms, opts?.signal)` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/runtime-env` (the same helper and import path as the merged #109710 Playwright-click and #109617 tab-discovery browser fixes), and the permissions route passes its `params.signal` through. An abort landing mid-backoff now rejects the sleep with the stable `Error("aborted")` from `sleepWithAbort`, which propagates out of `withCdpSocket` before any further socket is opened. Callers that pass no signal see zero behavior change — `sleepWithAbort(ms, undefined)` degenerates to the plain timer, and already-aborted signals are handled by the helper itself.

## Changes

- Thread an optional `signal` through `CdpSocketOptions`; handshake retry backoff sleeps via `sleepWithAbort`.
- Pass the request `signal` at the `grantPermissions` CDP call site.
- Regression test in `cdp.helpers.internal.test.ts`: a real `ws` `WebSocketServer` on 127.0.0.1 always rejects handshakes with 503; `withCdpSocket` runs with `handshakeRetries: 5` and a 30s retry delay; abort fires once the first rejection lands inside the backoff. Asserts rejection with `/aborted/`, wall clock under 10s, and exactly one handshake attempt (no second socket).

## User Impact

Cancelling a browser permission request (or its page/route operation timing out) while Chrome is unreachable no longer lingers through the remaining handshake retry backoff; the route tears down promptly instead of opening doomed sockets.

## Evidence

Exact head: `35432ce27de1131cccb352e8a82e099b191064dc`.

**Outside-runner behavior proof** — the production `withCdpSocket` is driven directly (no test runner, no mocks) via `node --import tsx` against a real loopback `ws` WebSocket server whose `verifyClient` rejects every handshake with 503 and counts attempts. The abort fires the moment the first rejected handshake lands inside the 3000ms backoff.

After fix — abort mid-backoff rejects in 1ms with the abort reason, exactly one handshake attempt, no second socket:

```text
$ TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=tsconfig.json node --import tsx /tmp/cdp-abort-proof.mts; echo "EXIT=$?"
[proof] loopback CDP WebSocket server: ws://127.0.0.1:40533/devtools/browser/TEST
[proof-server] handshake attempt #1 rejected with 503
[proof] AbortController.abort() fired at +29ms (inside 3000ms backoff)
[proof] outcome expect=after settled=rejected elapsedMs=30 abortAtMs=29 abortToRejectMs=1 handshakeAttempts=1 error="aborted"
[proof] check ok: withCdpSocket rejects (handshake never succeeds)
[proof] check ok: after-fix: rejection is the abort reason ("aborted")
[proof] check ok: after-fix: abort-to-reject 1ms < 1000ms (backoff was 3000ms)
[proof] check ok: after-fix: exactly one handshake attempt, no retry after abort (got 1)
[proof] OK
EXIT=0
```

Before fix (same script with `extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.ts` from `upstream/main`, restored immediately after): the abort at +12ms is ignored, handshake attempts #2 and #3 still fire on the full 3000ms schedule, and the rejection arrives 6135ms after the abort with the retry-exhaustion error instead of the abort reason.

```text
[proof-server] handshake attempt #1 rejected with 503
[proof] AbortController.abort() fired at +12ms (inside 3000ms backoff)
[proof-server] handshake attempt #2 rejected with 503
[proof-server] handshake attempt #3 rejected with 503
[proof] outcome expect=before settled=rejected elapsedMs=6147 abortAtMs=12 abortToRejectMs=6135 handshakeAttempts=3 error="Unexpected server response: 503"
[proof] check ok: before-fix: rejection is the retry-exhaustion failure, not the abort ("Unexpected server response: 503")
[proof] check ok: before-fix: abort ignored until backoff elapsed (6147ms >= 3000ms)
[proof] check ok: before-fix: retry fired despite the abort (attempts=3)
[proof] OK (expect=before)
```

Regression tests:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/cdp.helpers.internal.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  29 passed (29)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/permissions.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
```

Same new test against the pre-change implementation (file at `upstream/main`): the abort is ignored, the loop rides out the 30s backoff per attempt, and the run stalls until the 120s Vitest watchdog terminates it — the fixed implementation passes the same test in under 1s against a real loopback WebSocket server (no mocked fetch).

`oxlint` clean on all three changed files; `tsgo` extensions project reports no errors in browser files.

## Intentionally out of scope

- The other `withCdpSocket` call sites (`chrome.ts`, `cdp-page-session.ts`, `chrome.graphics.ts`, `pw-session.ts`, `cdp.ts`) keep their current no-signal behavior; this PR threads the signal only where a real per-request signal already exists and is checked around sibling stages.
- No change to retry counts, the 200ms→3s backoff schedule, jitter, or which handshake errors are retryable (rate-limited 429s still never retry).

target.title: fix(compaction): later provider timeouts discard completed chunks
target.body:
Related: #92043

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where multi-chunk compaction would discard summaries from completed chunks when a later provider request timed out, replacing useful progress with the generic "Summary unavailable due to size limits" fallback.

## Why This Change Was Made

Non-caller provider timeouts now use the existing partial-summary recovery path after at least one chunk has completed. Caller cancellation and wrapper safety-timeout aborts remain terminal, so this no longer changes post-timeout AgentSession persistence, lifecycle, or stored-state policy.

This update intentionally narrows the previous 20-file proposal to the primary contributor-owned invariant. The bounded post-timeout commit policy, session lifecycle drain, retained-entry remapping, timeout-helper cleanup, and failure-copy changes are no longer part of this PR.

## User Impact

When an early compaction chunk succeeds and a later provider request times out, OpenClaw retains the completed summary instead of losing all progress. Explicit cancellation behavior and the outer compaction safety timeout are unchanged.

## Evidence

The narrowed behavior is covered by a red/green regression test, adjacent compaction tests, and an actual loopback OpenAI-compatible HTTP/SSE before/after run.

### Real behavior proof

A loopback OpenAI-compatible HTTP/SSE provider exercised the production summary transport with two chunks: the first request returned a streamed summary and the second returned HTTP 504 with a provider timeout error.

- Before on `origin/main` (`277f009cc902aecf09ee0cdd8345223186c16fa9`): 2 provider requests; first chunk completed; later request timed out; `retainedCompletedChunk=false`; `partialMarkerPresent=false`; generic fallback returned.
- After on `1dc4de07426a218efe07d436d5db92bd1c7c37b8`: 2 provider requests; first chunk completed; later request timed out; `retainedCompletedChunk=true`; `partialMarkerPresent=true`; generic fallback absent.
- The proof used temporary loopback-only credentials and did not call a third-party provider.

### Tests and checks

- RED: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/compaction-partial-summary.test.ts` failed because a later timeout returned the generic fallback.
- GREEN: the same focused file passed, 9/9 tests.
- Adjacent compaction tests: `compaction-partial-summary.test.ts` plus `compaction.summarize-fallback.test.ts`, 13/13 tests passed.
- Formatting, conflict-marker, max-lines, dependency-pin, Plugin SDK API baseline, deprecated API, plugin-boundary, package-patch, and temp-creation checks passed.
- Local core typecheck was blocked by three unchanged `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` errors; the identical command reproduced the same errors on a clean `origin/main` control worktree with the same dependency tree.
- Structured autoreview built the final two-file bundle, but the Codex Responses WebSocket returned HTTP 403 before producing findings. The final diff was manually reviewed against `summarizeWithFallbackResult`, caller-abort behavior, timeout classification, and adjacent partial-summary tests.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound credential payload reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Lab credential add commands enforced `OPENCLAW_QA_CREDENTIAL_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` with a file stat before reading the payload. A payload file could grow after that stat and before the read, which let the command read and parse data beyond the configured cap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The credential payload reader now opens the file, verifies the opened handle is a regular file, and reads at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes from that handle. That keeps boundary-sized payload JSON accepted while rejecting files that are oversized at stat time or grow past the cap before the read, without reading the whole grown file into memory.

## User Impact

Operators using QA Lab credential pools get the configured payload byte limit applied to the actual bytes consumed by the CLI. Oversized or racing payload files fail before any credential broker request is sent.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.test.ts -- -t "credential payload"` passed: 1 file, 3 tests passed, 100 skipped.
- `git diff --check -- extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.ts extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.test.ts` passed.

target.title: fix: gateway boots when a configured plugin payload is broken
target.body:
Refs #109833

PR #110200 has merged into `main`; this branch is rebased onto its merge result.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where gateway readiness was blocked when a configured and enabled plugin package failed startup verification, even though the failure belonged to a known plugin surface that could be isolated.

## Why This Change Was Made

This implements the operator decision on #109833: degrade and boot. Startup quarantines the known plugin owner, emits its typed verification diagnostic once, and skips that plugin before any plugin code can load. Doctor, status, and health expose every quarantined plugin as `configured-unavailable`.

The behavior mirrors degraded SecretRef owners in `src/secrets/runtime-degraded-state.ts` and configured-unavailable channels in `src/channels/status/read-model.ts`. It also follows the root `AGENTS.md` security policy that failures isolate to the smallest known owning surface. The explicit `openclaw update` convergence path remains unchanged and continues to report payload convergence failures prominently.

## User Impact

Operators can keep the gateway ready when one configured plugin package is broken, while the broken plugin remains fully unavailable for that boot and its typed reason stays visible in operational diagnostics. State-migration failures, structurally invalid config, and startup failures with unknown ownership still block readiness.

## Summary

- Records enabled-plugin verification failures as a boot-stable quarantine snapshot refreshed on every Gateway process start.
- Prevents quarantined plugins from reaching artifact resolution or import.
- Keeps package-scoped peer-link inspection failures attached to known plugin ownership; inactive known packages do not block, while genuinely unowned failures remain blockers.
- Projects degraded state through doctor, status, and health, with install paths redacted from public diagnostics.
- Retains the quarantine diagnostic in registry/health state while emitting that exact typed finding only once during startup.

## Root Cause

Before this change, `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts` converted every plugin convergence warning into a fatal startup diagnostic. The design contract in `src/cli/update-cli/post-core-plugin-convergence.ts` explicitly required refusing restart whenever an active installed plugin payload was unloadable, so a known plugin-owned package failure blocked the entire gateway.

Real EACCES proof also exposed two adjacent causes that unit-only proof had missed:

- managed npm peer-link inspection read the same unreadable `package.json` first and converted that known package failure into an ownerless blocking warning;
- the startup migration checkpoint skipped plugin convergence on later processes, so a process-local quarantine could disappear on the second boot while the payload was still broken.

The fix preserves package ownership through peer inspection, refreshes plugin availability on every process start while leaving one-time state migrations checkpointed, and suppresses only the exact loader diagnostic already emitted by startup preflight. PR #110200 supplies the typed package-verification reasons, including unreadable `package.json`; this PR changes only the Gateway readiness policy for known plugin owners.

## Real behavior proof

Built-CLI local process proof on Linux with Node 25.9.0. The fixture is a packed npm plugin with `activation.onStartup: true`; its `register()` writes a sentinel and registers `proof-degrade.ping`. It was installed and enabled through the built CLI in an isolated temporary `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, then its installed `package.json` was changed to mode `000`. target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Hardening + cleanup on the MCP App sandbox CSP path, plus the root-cause fix for the diagnostics-listener CI flake.

1. **Decoder-owned fail-closed CSP validation.** #110275 restored the 400 for syntactically invalid `?csp=` JSON and #110264 added a handler-level guard for values that decode but do not normalize to a usable policy. This PR moves that invariant into `decodeMcpAppSandboxCsp` — the function that owns decode semantics — so any caller inherits fail-closed behavior: valid-JSON-but-not-a-CSP (base64url of `null`, `{}`, wrong-shaped objects) and explicitly empty (`?csp=`) values throw. The now-unreachable handler guard from #110264 is deleted. Endpoint behavior is unchanged from current main; the invariant has one owner and, unlike main today, regression tests.
2. **Non-isolated runner: reset the listener-presence mirror between files.** `resetOpenClawGlobalDiagnosticState` clears the diagnostic listener sets and deletes the state key, but the presence counts live under a separate `globalThis` record (`src/infra/diagnostic-event-listener-presence.ts`) and survived, so `hasInternalDiagnosticEventListeners()` stayed true for every later file in an `isolate:false` worker once any file leaked a registration. Concrete leak path: `src/logging/diagnostic-run-activity.ts` registers a listener at module-eval time; its stop handle dies with the module-registry reset. This flaked `model-call-diagnostics.test.ts` in run 29624203224 (`checks-node-compact-large-2`). #110288 landed the victim-side `beforeEach` reset; this fixes the class for every file in every non-isolated shard. Follow-up filed for removing the import-time registration itself.

> History note: this PR originally removed the stale-batch orphan tests and reverted the CSP guard; both were superseded (#110272, #110275) and the branch was rebased down to the remaining delta.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two malformed-CSP classes were found by Codex review while reverting the stale guard commit; the gaps predate it. One canonical owner for the invariant instead of a decoder/handler split, per repo policy. The runner fix removes a whole class of cross-file listener-state flakes.

## User Impact

The gateway MCP App sandbox endpoint keeps returning 400 for every malformed `?csp=` class (now tested); no behavior change for absent or valid parameters. CI: cross-file diagnostic listener leakage can no longer fail unrelated tests in non-isolated shards.

target.title: fix(browser): time out download saves
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Browser download waits used the configured timeout only until Playwright emitted the download event. After that event, the timer was cleared before `download.saveAs(...)` ran, so a stalled save could leave the browser tool call hanging indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

The download capture now removes the event listener when the download is observed, but keeps the original deadline active until the save operation settles. If the save hangs, the same timeout rejects the tool call instead of waiting forever.

## User Impact

Browser download tools now fail with the configured timeout when the browser starts a download but Playwright cannot finish saving it, making stalled downloads recoverable for agents and users.

Fixes an issue where users receiving iMessage image attachments could have attachment staging process a file larger than the configured inbound media limit when the source file grew after the initial filesystem size checks.

target.title: fix(ui): bound managed image blob URL fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts` fetches a managed chat image blob URL with `fetch(...)` **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled image endpoint hangs thumbnail resolution indefinitely.

Same unbounded-network-operation class as the many `fix(...)` "bound X" PRs: a request with no `AbortSignal` can block the caller forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the fetch in an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`MANAGED_IMAGE_BLOB_URL_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`, alongside the existing `MANAGED_IMAGE_BLOB_URL_MISS_RETRY_MS`), following the Control UI convention. The timer is cleared in `finally`.

## User Impact

Chat image thumbnails fail fast instead of hanging when the image endpoint is slow or down.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts` on `main` line 1552: `fetch(fetchUrl, { ... })` has no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into the request and clears the timeout.

Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>
## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Managed outgoing image blob resolution (`resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` in `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.ts`) hangs forever when the gateway image endpoint never responds, because the `fetch(fetchUrl, { ... })` call has no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24). The fix applies the same `AbortController` + `setTimeout(..., 30_000)` watchdog threaded into `fetch` as `signal`, cleared in `finally`, that PRs #110009 and #110010 already ship and prove with real local-HTTP-server tests (Nostr profile ops, chat avatar). #110009 / #110010 real-server tests: `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` and `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.test.ts` — both pass, showing a stalled endpoint aborts after the bound and a normal round trip still resolves.

Exact steps or command run after this patch (mode evidence):
- `node /Users/maomaoplanet/Projects/openclaw-evidence/pr-110011/repro.mjs`

Evidence after fix (standalone reproduction of the exact production fetch/signal/watchdog/clearTimeout pattern, using a 1s bound so it runs fast; production uses 30_000ms):
```
STALL  -> rejected: AbortError after 1004ms (bound 1000ms)
NORMAL -> resolved ok=true after 7ms
```

Observed result after fix: A stalled gateway endpoint is aborted via the `AbortController` watchdog (AbortError) instead of leaving the fetch pending forever; a responsive endpoint resolves normally. The production code path is identical to the already-proven #110009 / #110010 pattern, only the fetch target and 30s constant differ.

What was not tested: An in-repo Vitest unit test driving `resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` directly was not added because `chat-message.ts` statically imports browser-only components (`@awesome.me/webawesome` tooltips via `copy-button.ts`); the same import chain prevents the pre-existing `chat-message.test.ts` from loading in this environment (and in CI for this checkout), so a direct import test would only add a red job. The pattern itself is proven by the #110009 / #110010 real-server tests plus the standalone reproduction above.


---

## Additional test coverage (commit 4280253)

**Test file**: `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.ts`

**New tests**:
1. `it("aborts a stalled image fetch after the bound instead of hanging")` - Verifies AbortController terminates stalled fetch after 30s timeout
2. `it("still resolves a normal image fetch within timeout")` - Verifies normal fetch completes successfully
3. `it("returns null for network errors")` - Verifies network errors handled gracefully
4. `it("returns null for unauthorized requests (401)")` - Verifies 401 auth errors return null

**Test results**:
```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       99 passed (99) [including 4 new + 95 existing]
Duration    1.34s
```

**Pattern**: Same `AbortController` + `setTimeout(30_000)` watchdog as #110009 / #110010

**What was not tested**: Production E2E browser test (requires live gateway)

target.title: fix(google-video): cancel unread response body on download error
target.body:
## Summary

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw in `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` error path, so the unread response body stream is cancelled and the underlying connection is released immediately.

**What NOT changed**: No change to any other provider (OpenAI, Bedrock, etc.). No change to success paths. No change to retry or timeout logic. No new dependencies.

Fixes #109978

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` receives a non-OK HTTP response (e.g. 403, 429, 500), the `response.body` readable stream remains unconsumed. Node.js fetch keeps the TCP connection alive until the stream is GC'd or read to completion, causing connection stalls and resource leaks.

**Root Cause**: Missing `response.body.cancel()` in the error path of `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` in `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts`.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the error. The optional chaining handles null-body responses gracefully. The `.catch()` ensures the original download error is always thrown even if the cancel itself rejects.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic, Node.js v25.9.0, OpenClaw 2026.7.2

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Run the unit test suite to confirm existing behavior
cd /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/google/video-generation-provider.test.ts

# Run the dedicated evidence script that simulates body cancel scenarios
npx tsx scripts/evidence-video.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
=== HEAD commit ===
bb946de5cf8 fix(google-video): cancel unread response body on download error

--- Body cancel on error path ---
Body cancel executed: YES ✅
Error: Download failed: 403 Forbidden

--- Original error preserved ---
Body cancel attempted: YES ✅
Error: Video generation failed (500)

--- Null body (optional chaining) ---
Null body handled: YES (via ?.) ✅
Error: Bad request

--- All HTTP error status codes ---
Status 400: body cancelled=OK ✅
Status 401: body cancelled=OK ✅
Status 403: body cancelled=OK ✅
Status 429: body cancelled=OK ✅
Status 500: body cancelled=OK ✅
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All body cancel scenarios pass. The body is cancelled before throw for all HTTP error status codes. The original download error is preserved even when `body.cancel()` rejects. Null-body responses are safely handled by optional chaining without throwing.

**What was not tested**: Real HTTP fetch to an actual Google Cloud endpoint (the error path is hard to trigger without invalid credentials / rate limiting; the fix pattern is verified at the logic level).

## Tests and validation

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
   Start at  07:10:38
   Duration  18.89s (transform 15.27s, setup 573ms, import 18.08s, tests 103ms, environment 0ms)
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

Sibling sandbox/execution plugins (openshell, acpx, codex) already ship this metadata, so MXC was inconsistent and harder to configure safely. ## Why This Change Was Made Adds cheap, behavior-neutral manifest metadata to `extensions/mxc/openclaw.plugin.json` (mirrored from the Zod config schema so the manifest↔schema drift test stays green): - **`configContracts.dangerousFlags`** flags `network: "default"` — the one setting that actually weakens isolation (it flips the container to allow outbound egress via the `internetClient` capability). `containment` is intentionally **not** flagged, because `"process"` and `"processcontainer"` currently both resolve to the same Windows ProcessContainer. - **Per-field `uiHints`** (label / help / advanced) for all six config fields. - **Field `description`s** on the config schema, added via `.describe()` in `src/config.ts` and mirrored into the manifest. - Manifest `description` aligned with the plugin entry.
